title: PHY-less bonding: sense amplifiers drive logic registers directly
idea: Ideal: memory bits appear in the processor's registers with no interface at all. Closest achievable: hybrid-bond the DRAM array face-down onto logic at 1-2 um pitch so each sense-amp latch connects through its own bond to a logic-side flip-flop, deleting DQ drivers, SerDes, DLLs and the global data bus.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and periphery (fact 7): link energy drops from 3-4 pJ/bit (HBM) toward ~0.05 pJ/bit, and I/O plus global-bus periphery (~10-15% of die) disappears.

title: Mat-granular bond clusters for 64-byte, zero-overfetch activation
idea: Ideal: fetch exactly the byte asked for and nothing else. Closest achievable: give every 512x512 mat its own cluster of hybrid-bond pads for local wordline enable and data, so the logic die activates a single mat segment instead of an 8 KB page spread across 16 mats.
why: Fact 8 overfetch: 128x overfetch falls to ~8x and random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.6 pJ; fewer cells disturbed per ACT also eases row hammer (fact 9).

title: Interposer decoupling trenches repurposed as gigabyte-class eDRAM
idea: Ideal: the package's dead silicon stores data for free. Closest achievable: passive silicon interposers already carry deep-trench decoupling capacitors; add a 65-90 nm access transistor per trench plus simple sense periphery so the ~2,500 mm2 interposer becomes a ~0.5-1 GB eDRAM L4 directly under the HBM and GPU.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: built on depreciated 65 nm lines with no EUV (fact 4); absorbs hot traffic before it crosses into HBM (fact 5) and adds capacity per package from area already paid for.

title: Blow-away ESD shunts after bonding to strip I/O capacitance
idea: Ideal: die-to-die wires with zero parasitic load. Closest achievable: replace each inter-die pad's ESD diode stack (~0.2-0.5 pF) with one shared sacrificial shunt network that protects only during handling and bonding, then laser- or electrically fuse it open after the stack is sealed, leaving ~10 fF bond loads.
why: Facts 5 and 6: link energy scales with C, so removing ESD load cuts per-bit energy 5-10x on hybrid-bond and TSV lanes and shrinks pad area so more lanes fit per mm2.

title: Transferred micron-thin array films replace thinned TSV dies
idea: Ideal: stacking costs no silicon area at all. Closest achievable: instead of thinning HBM dies to 30-50 um and drilling 5-10 um TSVs with keep-out zones, smart-cut a 1-2 um device film of each DRAM array and bond it sequentially, linking tiers with ~0.5 um nano-vias that need almost no keep-out.
why: Fact 6 TSV tax: via plus keep-out area falls from several % of die to <0.5%; stack height shrinks so 24-32 tiers fit the current 720 um envelope, with lower thermal resistance.

title: TSV-free cube stacking with sidewall-printed interconnect
idea: Ideal: a memory stack with no holes in it. Closest achievable: route each DRAM die's bus to one edge, stack dies like playing cards, polish the stack face and pattern a 2 um redistribution layer across the exposed edges so all vertical wiring lives on the sidewall outside the silicon.
why: Fact 6: eliminates TSV etch, fill and reveal and their share of the 20-30% stack yield loss and area tax; uses planar tools only and lets dies be sorted before assembly.

title: MicroLED imaging-fiber links: each pixel a memory bit lane
idea: Ideal: thousands of wires with no wires. Closest achievable: put ~10,000 GaN microLEDs and silicon photodiodes on the DRAM base die, couple them into a coherent imaging fiber bundle and land it on a matching array on the GPU, each pixel carrying 2-4 Gb/s NRZ with no SerDes, lasers or modulators.
why: Fact 5: ~0.5-1 pJ/bit at metre reach with no retimers, so memory can leave the package and the interposer (fact 6) shrinks; no EUV and no III-V lasers needed.

title: Wavelength is the address: passive AWG-routed photonic memory pool
idea: Ideal: addressing that costs no logic and no switching energy. Closest achievable: the host tunes a comb line whose wavelength encodes the target bank, a passive arrayed-waveguide grating steers that light to the bank's receiver, and the reply returns on the same wavelength, so bank selection needs no electronic switch or decoder tree.
why: Facts 5 and 7: removes switch, arbiter and decoder energy and area for pooled memory; latency is time of flight (~5 ns/m), keeping a rack-scale pool within DRAM-class access.

title: Frequency-division memory bus: every bank owns a carrier
idea: Ideal: all banks talk at once on one wire. Closest achievable: each bank's I/O modulates its own RF carrier slot (2-40 GHz) onto a single shared interposer transmission line, and the controller demodulates all channels at once with a wideband ADC plus FFT, replacing hundreds of parallel traces.
why: Fact 6 and interposer cost: cuts trace and bump count ~16x, reducing interposer layers and area while enabling full bank-parallel access without wide buses.

title: Resonant interposer bus that recycles line charge every cycle
idea: Ideal: moving a bit costs zero energy. Closest achievable: integrate spiral inductors in the interposer so each memory data line resonates with its own capacitance; bits are encoded as the phase of a resonant swing and 60-80% of the CV2 energy sloshes back each cycle instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Fact 5 and fact 10 voltage floor: link energy falls 3-5x without lowering voltage, beating the CV2 wall by recovery rather than scaling.

title: Optical weight carousel: one circulating copy feeds sixty-four GPUs
idea: Ideal: model weights exist exactly once in the whole cluster. Closest achievable: stream frozen weights continuously around a WDM fiber loop at ~10 Tb/s so each GPU taps its current layer as it passes, holding only a small double buffer instead of a full weight replica in HBM.
why: Usable supply: 64 data-parallel replicas of a 400 GB model collapse toward one, freeing tens of TB of HBM for KV cache and trading scarce DRAM for cheap fiber and optics.

title: Exponent-plane storage: base die dedups bf16 exponents
idea: Ideal: store only information, never redundancy. Closest achievable: the HBM base die transparently splits bf16/fp8 tensors into sign-mantissa planes and an exponent plane, entropy-codes the low-entropy exponents (~2.5 bits instead of 8) and reassembles them at line rate on read.
why: Usable capacity and bandwidth: ~25-30% more effective HBM capacity and interface bandwidth for AI tensors with no host changes; fewer bits moved per useful value (fact 5).

title: Index-list gather engine returns only packed useful words
idea: Ideal: the memory already knows which words you need. Closest achievable: the host sends a list of 4-8 byte indices (embedding rows, sparse nonzeros, KV pages) over the command path, and the base die does bank-parallel fetches and returns densely packed 64 B lines holding only the requested words.
why: Fact 8 and fact 5: sparse and embedding workloads waste 80-95% of transferred bytes; packing cuts interface traffic 5-10x for those patterns.

title: Uploaded access programs delete the DRAM command bus
idea: Ideal: no requests at all, data simply arrives on time. Closest achievable: compilers for static AI graphs emit a timed access program (tile addresses, strides, bank schedule) once per layer, and a tiny sequencer in the base die replays it so the per-access command/address bus and controller queues vanish.
why: Facts 5 and 7: command/address bumps (~20% of HBM signal bumps) become data bumps, GPU controller area and energy shrink, and conflict-free schedules push bandwidth utilization toward 95%.

title: N-plus-one HBM: a spare die rewired in after stacking
idea: Ideal: stacking never wastes a good die. Closest achievable: build 13-high stacks sold as 12-high, with a crossbar of redundant TSV lanes in the base die so any one failing core die or TSV column is mapped out at final test.
why: Fact 6: converts 20-30% stack yield loss into a fixed ~8% capacity overhead; stack yield rises toward 90%+, cutting HBM cost per good bit ~15-20%.

title: Panel-scale glass interposers replacing reticle-stitched silicon
idea: Ideal: interposers as cheap as window glass. Closest achievable: build redistribution layers and through-glass vias on 510x515 mm glass panels with LCD-style lithography, giving ~6x the area per process pass of a 300 mm wafer with flatness good enough for 2 um lines.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: reuses display tools and domestic glass supply; interposer cost per package falls ~3-5x and the reticle-size limit disappears, allowing more HBM sites per GPU.

title: Aerogel thermal moat between hot logic and memory stack
idea: Ideal: memory stacked on logic yet as cold as if it were far away. Closest achievable: a 20-50 um silica-aerogel or vacuum-gap layer, pierced only by thin copper signal pillars, thermally isolates DRAM tiers from the logic die while a separate cold plate cools the DRAM from its own side.
why: Facts 3 and 5: memory-on-logic normally heats DRAM and doubles refresh per ~10 C; keeping DRAM below ~50 C halves refresh and makes zero-distance stacking practical.

title: Plastic sub-terahertz waveguide ribbons replace copper memory channels
idea: Ideal: a memory channel with no copper loss. Closest achievable: run D-band (110-170 GHz) carriers through polymer dielectric waveguide ribbons between the GPU package and memory modules up to ~1 m, launched by CMOS on-die couplers, so memory can sit off-package without optics.
why: Fact 5: ~1-2 pJ/bit beyond-package reach vs 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 channels; decouples capacity from package area (fact 6) using cheap plastic and plain CMOS.

title: Single optical clock broadcast removes clock-recovery from memory links
idea: Ideal: every chip already knows when each bit will arrive. Closest achievable: distribute one low-jitter mode-locked optical clock to all memory and compute chiplets through a passive splitter tree, making every link source-synchronous to a common reference with no CDR, DLL or link training.
why: Facts 5 and 7: CDR/DLL is ~20-40% of SerDes energy and area; removing it cuts link energy ~30% and lets links wake in nanoseconds instead of microseconds.

title: Rack spot market for stranded memory, priced per GB-second
idea: Ideal: no gigabyte sits idle anywhere. Closest achievable: CXL-attached rack memory pools publish idle capacity to a scheduler that leases it per GB-second to neighbouring servers, migrating cold pages at ~10 ms granularity and reclaiming on demand.
why: Usable supply: 25-40% of server DRAM is stranded at any moment; recovering half of it raises effective fleet supply 12-20% without new wafers.

title: Open UCIe memory-chiplet standard to admit second-source DRAM makers
idea: Ideal: any memory die works with any processor. Closest achievable: define an open die-to-die DRAM chiplet interface (UCIe-based, with a standard base-die command set, thermal limits and test protocol) so new or smaller U.S. memory fabs can sell bare array chiplets into anyone's package without building their own base die or PHY.
why: Supply concentration and U.S. manufacturability: lowers the entry ticket from full HBM stacks to bare arrays and widens the supplier base beyond three companies.

title: U.S. stacking hubs: import arrays, add value through hybrid bonding
idea: Ideal: the U.S. gains DRAM capacity without first building a $15B fab. Closest achievable: fund domestic advanced-packaging hubs that buy known-good DRAM wafers from several allied fabs and do thinning, hybrid bonding, base-die attach and test in the U.S., later becoming the integration point for U.S.-made arrays.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: packaging lines cost ~$1-3B and 18-24 months vs 3-5 years for a fab, capture ~40-50% of HBM value, and relieve the stacking-capacity part of the HBM bottleneck.

title: Predictive link coding: both ends guess, only residuals travel
idea: Ideal: send nothing because the receiver already knows. Closest achievable: run an identical tiny predictor (per-stream stride/delta or last-value) in the base die and the GPU PHY, transmit only XOR residuals with run-length coding, and resync on mismatch, like a video codec for memory traffic.
why: Fact 5: for smooth activations, KV cache and pointer-heavy data 30-60% of transferred bits are predictable, cutting link toggles and I/O energy by a similar fraction.

title: Read-as-refresh: scheduler guarantees every live row is touched
idea: Ideal: memory that never needs refreshing because it is always in use. Closest achievable: in LLM decode every weight and resident KV entry is read once per token, so the serving scheduler caps step time below 32 ms, lays tensors so each step activates every occupied row, and the base die verifies row coverage and issues no REF; sequences that go idle are evicted rather than kept.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) and the 10-20% bandwidth loss go to zero for decode-dominated serving because ordinary activate-restore does the job for free.

title: TTL-tagged allocations: data declared dead before it can decay
idea: Ideal: data lives exactly as long as it is needed. Closest achievable: add a time-to-live field to the memory allocation interface; regions tagged TTL < retention (activations, gradient buckets, collective-comm buffers, scratch) go to banks whose refresh circuits are disabled, and the base die faults any access arriving after expiry.
why: Fact 3: in training a majority of HBM traffic and much capacity is transient data with microsecond-to-millisecond lifetimes; those bits never pay refresh energy or bandwidth.

title: Retention-bounded FIFO DRAM die with no row decoders
idea: Ideal: a memory that is a pipe, holding data only while it flows. Closest achievable: a streaming DRAM die organized as a circular buffer of rows driven by a sequential row counter, sized so wrap-around time is below retention; it has no random row decoder, no refresh counter and only a head/tail pointer interface, serving as the staging buffer between flash or remote memory and the GPU.
why: Zero refresh by construction plus fact 7: removing decoders and refresh logic recovers ~15-20% of die area; fits weight streaming and pipeline-parallel buffers.

title: Millisecond DRAM: tiny capacitors legal because data dies young
idea: Ideal: a capacitor that stores just enough charge for exactly as long as needed. Closest achievable: specify a die class with ~1 fF cells (aspect ratio ~15:1 instead of 60-75:1) guaranteed for only ~2 ms retention, sold exclusively behind a TTL/streaming interface that refuses allocations longer than 1 ms, so it is never refreshed.
why: Fact 1 capacitor wall and fact 4: shallow capacitors drop the costliest etch and deposition steps, raise yield and allow ~1.5-2x density at the same node, with refresh energy zero by contract.

title: Let it rot: detect decayed lines and recompute instead
idea: Ideal: never spend energy keeping data you could regenerate. Closest achievable: KV cache and activation checkpoints sit in unrefreshed DRAM with a strong per-line checksum; when a line decays the base die flags it and the runtime recomputes it from upstream tokens or inputs instead of ever rewriting it.
why: Fact 3: zero refresh power for regenerable data, trading occasional recompute FLOPs (abundant) for retention energy and bandwidth (scarce); the leakage tail becomes a performance statistic, not a reliability wall.

title: Significance split: MSBs in static cells, LSBs allowed to fade
idea: Ideal: protect only the bits that matter. Closest achievable: the base die bit-slices each fp8/bf16 word so sign, exponent and top mantissa bits go to on-logic SRAM while low mantissa bits go to never-refreshed DRAM, where decay toward zero acts as graceful rounding noise for neural-network tensors.
why: Fact 3: zero refresh power with bounded numerical error (<0.5% relative per decayed value); ~50-60% of bits live in cheap DRAM and the rest in SRAM already present on the base die.

title: Age-out tiering: base die evicts rows before retention, never refreshes
idea: Ideal: every row is either fresh or gone. Closest achievable: the HBM base die keeps a per-row age counter; rows nearing ~50 ms without natural access are compressed and written once to a dense non-volatile tier (stacked NAND or a remote pool) and the DRAM row is freed, making DRAM a pure write-back cache of recent data with no REF command.
why: Fact 3: refresh power goes to zero and idle DRAM can be fully powered off; long-lived cold data costs one write instead of ~16 refreshes per second forever.

title: Cryogenic memory pod linked optically to warm compute
idea: Ideal: charge that never leaks. Closest achievable: immerse DRAM stacks in liquid nitrogen (77 K), where access-transistor leakage falls by orders of magnitude and retention exceeds hours, and connect them to room-temperature GPUs only by optical fiber so no copper heat leak or thermal mismatch crosses the boundary; refresh is disabled.
why: Fact 3: refresh power to zero; cold wires also cut resistive loss and permit ~0.5 V arrays (fact 10), with cryocooler overhead paid only on the small memory heat load.

title: Via-ROM weight stacks written by maskless direct-write
idea: Ideal: frozen model weights stored with zero energy and zero masks. Closest achievable: build via-programmed ROM arrays at 28 nm whose single programming via layer is written per model by multi-beam e-beam direct-write, stack 8-16 dies in an HBM footprint and hybrid-bond them to the accelerator so weights stream with no refresh and no write path.
why: Zero refresh, no capacitor (fact 1), no EUV (fact 4) and ~2-4x cheaper per bit than DRAM on depreciated 28 nm lines; frees HBM for KV cache.

title: Field-programmed antifuse stacks: burn weights through the memory interface
idea: Ideal: a memory you write once at deployment and never maintain. Closest achievable: multi-layer antifuse crosspoint dies (gate-oxide breakdown with diode select, 4F2 per layer) are programmed in place through the accelerator's own memory channels when a model is deployed, then served read-only with no refresh and no standby power.
why: Zero refresh and no per-model masks; stacked crosspoint OTP on mature nodes reaches DRAM-competitive density, and endurance is irrelevant for frozen weights.

title: Charge-trap NOR weight towers hybrid-bonded under the GPU
idea: Ideal: weights that persist with no power and arrive at DRAM speed. Closest achievable: stack 3D charge-trap NOR (vertical channels, ~100 ns random read, wide parallel pages) in an HBM-shaped tower, hybrid-bond it to the base die, and use it only as a read-mostly weight store updated at deployment.
why: Zero refresh, ~5-10x DRAM bits per mm2 through vertical layering, and NAND-style tooling already in U.S. fabs; DRAM demand drops by the weight share of inference memory (often 50-70%).

title: Eight-tier hybrid-bonded SRAM towers as the hot tier
idea: Ideal: a static memory as big as DRAM. Closest achievable: stack 8 thinned SRAM-only dies (no logic) with 1 um hybrid bonds directly over compute, each ~100 mm2 tier holding ~150 MB at 3 nm-class density, giving ~1 GB of refresh-free, sub-5 ns, ~0.1 pJ/bit storage per stack for hot KV pages and activations.
why: Zero refresh power and ~30x lower movement energy than HBM (fact 5); draws on logic-fab capacity, which is more abundant than DRAM capacity, and absorbs the hottest 5-10% of the working set.

title: Volume-holographic weight crystals read by light into compute
idea: Ideal: weights held in a passive crystal and read by a flash of light. Closest achievable: record each layer's weight pages as angle-multiplexed holograms in a photopolymer or LiNbO3 block; a steered laser reconstructs one ~1 Mb page per pulse onto a photodiode array bonded to the accelerator, with no refresh and no electrical storage.
why: Zero refresh and page-parallel Tb/s reads of frozen weights at low pJ/bit; TB-per-cm3 class capacity offloads weights from DRAM entirely, though random access is microseconds, so it suits streaming.

title: Retention-binned stacks with weak-row exile and sub-second rewrite cadence
idea: Ideal: every cell holds charge as well as the best cell. Closest achievable: at stack test, measure each row's retention and remap the weakest ~0.1% (the 13 fA tail) to base-die SRAM spares so the stack guarantees >=2 s retention, then dedicate it to training jobs whose optimizer step rewrites all weights, gradients and moments in under 1 s, with refresh switched off.
why: Fact 3: retention is set by the tail; exiling it lifts guaranteed retention ~30x so the natural rewrite cadence removes refresh power and the 10-20% bandwidth tax.

title: Ephemeral-memory cloud SKU: cheap RAM that forgets after 50 ms
idea: Ideal: users pay only for memory during the instant they use it. Closest achievable: a cloud instance class exposes a large never-refreshed 'ephemeral memory' region whose contents are guaranteed only 50 ms after the last write, priced ~40% lower, with SDKs for streaming ETL, video, AI activations and network buffers that fit the contract.
why: Zero refresh power on the ephemeral tier, and providers can fill it with DRAM dies that fail standard retention bins, salvaging 5-10% more usable supply from existing output.

title: Spatial pipelining: activations ride chip-to-chip links, never parking
idea: Ideal: data is always moving and never at rest, so nothing has to be retained. Closest achievable: map a model layer-per-chiplet across a wafer or board so activations stream over short die-to-die links from one tile's SRAM buffer to the next, with weights pinned in each tile's local static storage and no DRAM holding activations.
why: Zero refresh power and fact 5: ~0.1 pJ/bit per hop vs 3-4 pJ/bit for an HBM round trip; DRAM demand for activations falls to zero.

title: Latching NEMS relay tiles: bits held by mechanical contact
idea: Ideal: a bit held forever with zero leakage, by geometry instead of charge. Closest achievable: a chiplet of nanoelectromechanical relays with adhesion-latched bistable cantilevers in vacuum-sealed wafer-level cavities, written by a 1-3 V pulse and read by contact resistance in ~10 ns, bonded under the GPU as a static scratchpad.
why: Zero refresh and zero standby leakage, no capacitor (fact 1) and no access-transistor tail (fact 3); buildable in mature U.S. MEMS fabs, though contact endurance is the open risk.

title: Procedural weights: generator at the interposer synthesizes tensors from seeds
idea: Ideal: weights that take no storage because they are computed on demand. Closest achievable: train models whose weight matrices are a small stored core plus pseudo-random projections regenerated at line rate by a hash/PRNG engine in the base die or interposer, so only seeds and cores (~5-10% of bits) live in static storage.
why: Zero refresh because the stored state fits in SRAM or ROM, and 10-20x fewer bits moved; trades abundant logic for scarce DRAM capacity and bandwidth.

title: Park KV caches in network-switch SRAM across the rack
idea: Ideal: storage that already exists and sits idle. Closest achievable: modern switch ASICs carry ~100-200 MB of SRAM packet buffer that is mostly empty at moderate load; reserve part of it as a rack-wide static parking lot for KV pages of paused conversations, addressed by RDMA-like verbs and evicted under congestion.
why: Zero refresh power for parked state and new capacity from silicon already deployed (dozens of switches per pod at 100+ MB each), relieving HBM pressure from idle sessions.

title: Memory retention energy metric in data-center efficiency codes
idea: Ideal: refresh waste is visible and priced. Closest achievable: add a standardized 'retention energy per stored GB-hour' metric, read from DRAM REF counters, to federal data-center efficiency reporting and procurement alongside PUE, with procurement preference for systems that reach zero refresh on declared workloads.
why: Creates market pull for zero-refresh architectures, since refresh is 16-33% of idle DRAM power and roughly 1-3% of IT energy; a cheap policy lever.

title: Superconducting persistent-current loops behind an optical cryostat window
idea: Ideal: a current that circulates forever with no supply. Closest achievable: store bits as flux quanta in niobium persistent-current loops at 4 K (Josephson memory arrays) driven by on-cryostat SFQ logic, with data entering and leaving through optical fiber links to warm processors.
why: Zero refresh and zero static power at the cell with aJ-class writes; costs are cryocooler power, poor cell density and closed-cycle helium use, which conflicts with the helium chokepoint.

title: Vector-quantized KV cache sized to fit base-die SRAM
idea: Ideal: the working set shrinks until static memory can hold it. Closest achievable: the base die encodes each KV vector as 2-4 indices into learned per-head codebooks (product quantization), shrinking the KV cache 8-16x so the hot cache fits in base-die SRAM, and computes attention scores directly on the codes.
why: Zero refresh power for the KV tier and 8-16x less KV traffic (fact 5); KV cache is the fastest-growing DRAM consumer in long-context inference.

title: Vacuum-gap floating electrodes in hermetic cavities hold charge for years
idea: Ideal: a capacitor with no leakage path at all. Closest achievable: each cell is a micro-electrode suspended in a wafer-level vacuum cavity with no dielectric to tunnel through, charged by a field-emission tip on write and sensed capacitively by an underlying transistor gate without contact, so stored charge persists for years without refresh.
why: Facts 1 and 3: removes both the dielectric and junction leakage paths that force refresh; hermetic vacuum packaging becomes the memory technology itself.
